by_task.procedure: Treat statutory dollar limits as protection ceilings, not eligibility tests: a firearm may qualify under § 33-1125(10) and a motor vehicle under § 33-1125(8) even when its value exceeds the limit. Use § 33-1125(9) for a professionally authorized prosthesis or assistive medical device, including medical monitoring equipment and motorized mobility devices. Assess each listed vehicle independently. Use § 33-1125(4) only for engagement or wedding rings and § 33-1125(1) only for wearing apparel.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not treat an ordinary household appliance as a medical aid, extend the ring exemption to other jewelry, classify jewelry as apparel, or list administrative rules such as §§ 33-1101(B), 33-1121, or 33-1133(B) as asset exemptions.

by_task.when: Arizona exemptions are allowable and an asset satisfies the stated property category.
by_task.procedure: For each independent alternative, claim no more than the asset value and the applicable ceiling: $15,000 for a motor vehicle, $2,000 aggregate for firearms, and $2,000 aggregate for engagement and wedding rings. A qualifying over-limit asset remains eligible at the capped amount.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not award the ring ceiling to bracelets, necklaces, pendants, or other jewelry, and do not add administrative provisions as separate claim alternatives.

operations.rationale: In source 299 EC the parent omitted § 33-1125(9) for provider-issued medical monitoring equipment although the released target applies that provision; source 207 supplies the same benchmark boundary for a physician-authorized assistive device. This adds the omitted medical condition without changing unrelated Arizona value rules.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are allowable and an asset is tested under 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(2), (d)(3), or (d)(4).
by_task.procedure: Decide the property category without comparing value to its ceiling. Use § 522(d)(2) for a motor vehicle, § 522(d)(3) for listed household goods, furnishings, apparel, appliances, books, animals, crops, or musical instruments, and § 522(d)(4) only for jewelry. A qualifying category remains eligible above its dollar limit.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not classify firearms under § 522(d)(3), treat a container or furnishing as jewelry merely because it stores jewelry, or omit a vehicle, household item, or musical instrument because its value exceeds the ceiling.

operations.rationale: The parent omitted § 522(d)(3) from over-limit household and musical-instrument categories in source 291, treated a household organizer as jewelry in source 298, and omitted the over-limit motor-vehicle provision in source 306. The repair separates category eligibility from valuation and adds the previously absent § 522(d)(2) boundary.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are an allowable namespace and the asset is property of the estate.
by_task.procedure: After checking the asset-specific paragraphs, independently add 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5) for every asset because it covers any property. Before finalizing, check each asset separately and retain this alternative even when a specific Federal or state exemption also applies. A dollar ceiling limits value, not EC eligibility.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are allowable and valuing the independent 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5) alternative.
by_task.procedure: Always report § 522(d)(5) separately for every asset, including an asset also eligible under § 522(d)(1) or another specific paragraph. Unless the facts state that § 522(d)(1) has actually consumed an amount, claim the lesser of asset value and $15,425 for one debtor. For equally owned joint property, return one combined asset-level amount equal to the lesser of the full asset value and $30,850.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit the wildcard because a specific exemption applies, halve jointly owned asset value, stop at one spouse's $15,425 ceiling for joint property, use only the $1,475 base without stated homestead consumption, or use it outside the Federal namespace.

operations.rationale: Current EV outputs omitted the wildcard from otherwise specifically exempt property in sources 303 and 305 and used half-value or one-debtor amounts for joint property in sources 291 and 306. This narrowly replaces the ambiguous half-by-half instruction with the released asset-level joint calculation while preserving the established independent-alternative rule.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and the asset is personal property used personally rather than for business.
by_task.procedure: For each personal-property asset, first add 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b), then add any qualifying specific subsection; never replace subsection (b) with the specific alternative. This includes jewelry, vehicles, household property, health aids, and necessary wearing apparel. Add subsection (a) only for necessary wearing apparel, Bibles, school books, or family pictures, and subsection (e) only for professionally prescribed health aids.

by_task.avoid_when: Do not apply subsection (b) to real property, halve jointly owned asset value, omit subsection (b) from jewelry or apparel, infer subsection (d) trade use without explicit business facts, report zero-value alternatives, or double the $2,400 vehicle ceiling.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are allowable and a personal-property asset satisfies a specific category in § 18.345(1).

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are allowable and the debtor has an interest in the asset.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are allowable and valuing the independent § 8123 alternative.
by_task.procedure: Report one asset-level § 8123 amount: the lesser of full asset value and $300 for one debtor, or the lesser of full asset value and $600 for jointly owned property of two debtors.

by_task.when: Wisconsin exemptions are allowable and an asset is tested as a consumer good, motor vehicle, or occupied homestead.
